sections.h2: Does Iowa have a separate capital gains tax on a house sale?
sections.html:
No. Iowa does not charge a stand-alone capital gains tax. The profit from selling a house is reported as part of your Iowa individual income tax return, and for tax year 2026 the Department of Revenue says one flat rate of 3.8 percent applies to all levels of taxable income.

On the Iowa return, the capital gain or loss line starts with 100 percent of the amount from your federal Form 1040. The state says the capital gain deduction is not taken on that line, because a qualifying deduction goes on a separate line. If your federal return needs Schedule D and Form 8949, a copy goes with the Iowa return.

One note to avoid confusion: the 3.8 percent Iowa rate and the 3.8 percent federal net investment income tax share a number and nothing else. They are separate taxes with separate rules, and both can matter on a large gain.

sections.h2: How much gain on your Iowa home can you exclude?
sections.html:
If the house was your main home, you can generally exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. Iowa says it generally follows the federal rules on excluding gain from a principal residence, so the federal exclusion also keeps that gain off your Iowa taxable income.

The IRS sets two tests, and you must meet both:

  • Ownership: you or your spouse owned the home for at least 24 months of the five years before the sale.
  • Use: you, and your spouse if filing jointly, each lived in it as a main home for at least 24 months of that same five-year period.

The two 24-month periods do not need to be the same months. Generally you cannot use the exclusion if you excluded gain from another home sale during the two years before this one. The IRS points to Publication 523 for exceptions and partial exclusions.

You must report the sale if you receive a Form 1099-S, even if the full gain is excludable, and if you cannot exclude all of the gain. Use Form 8949 with Schedule D.

sections.h2: What happens if the gain is larger than the exclusion?
sections.html:
Gain above the exclusion is taxed federally as a capital gain and in Iowa at the flat state rate. The federal rate depends on how long you held the property.

ItemRule from the source
Held one year or lessShort-term, taxed as ordinary income
Held more than one yearLong-term, federal rates of 0, 15 or 20 percent by taxable income
Unrecaptured section 1250 gain (depreciation on real property)Maximum federal rate of 25 percent
Iowa individual income tax, 20263.8 percent flat
Iowa interest on overdue tax, from January 1, 202610 percent a year, 0.8 percent a month

The federal net investment income tax is 3.8 percent for single filers above $200,000, joint filers above $250,000 and separate filers above $125,000 of modified adjusted gross income. The IRS says the tax does not apply to the part of a home sale gain that is excluded as a principal residence. Gain above the exclusion can be hit.

sections.h2: Which Iowa capital gain deductions were repealed?
sections.html:
Most Iowa capital gain deductions ended with tax year 2023. The Department of Revenue states that the repealed categories include gains from selling real estate used in a non-farm business, an entire business, timber, cattle, horses or breeding livestock (with an exception for retired farmers), and employer securities sold to a qualified Iowa employee stock ownership plan.

The change took effect January 1, 2023. Installment sales that began before that date still qualify for the deduction. The Department's deduction page still carries reference material for non-farm real property, but the state's 2023 changes page controls, and the statute governs in any dispute.

That matters to anyone who read older guidance that gave a ten-year holding rule for business real estate. If you sold rental or commercial property after 2022, do not rely on it.

  • Retired farmers aged 55 or older may still deduct gain from farm real estate if they materially participated in farming for ten years in total.
  • A retired farmer has a single lifetime election.
  • Electing the deduction blocks the beginning farmer tax credit and the farm lease income exclusion.
  • Gain from an employee-owned corporation's stock has its own phase-in: 33 percent excluded for 2023, 66 percent for 2024 and 100 percent from 2025.

A house in town or a rental house is not covered by those farm rules. A principal residence relies on the federal exclusion instead.

sections.h2: How does an inherited Iowa house change the gain?
sections.html:
Inherited property generally takes a new tax basis equal to its fair market value on the date of the owner's death, not the price the deceased originally paid. A sale soon after inheritance often produces little or no taxable gain for that reason.

The estate's personal representative can instead elect an alternate valuation date, which uses the value on that date. If you did not receive a Schedule A (Form 8971), the IRS says you can use the appraised value at death for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes. Property given to the decedent within one year before death can carry the decedent's adjusted basis rather than the death-date value.

Keep an appraisal from the date of death. It is the first document a tax preparer will ask for if you sell a house you inherited in Iowa, and it is hard to recreate later.

sections.h2: Do nonresidents owe Iowa tax on a house they sell in Iowa?
sections.html:
Yes, if the Iowa-source income reaches the filing trigger. The Department of Revenue lists capital gain on the sale of Iowa property, along with rental income, as income from Iowa property. A nonresident or part-year resident must file when Iowa-source net income is $1,000 or more, unless income falls under the standard thresholds.

For the 2025 return year those thresholds were more than $9,000 for single or married filing separately filers, and more than $13,500 for joint filers, head of household and qualifying surviving spouse. Higher amounts apply to people 65 and older.

People who sell an Iowa house after moving away, or heirs living out of state, often miss this step. Check it before the money is spent.

sections.h2: What other Iowa costs show up when a house is sold?
sections.html:
Iowa property tax and state transfer tax are separate from any income tax on the gain. Real estate transfer tax applies to a deed that conveys Iowa real estate when the consideration exceeds $500, at 80 cents for each $500 or fractional part above $500, under Iowa Code 428A.1. The code treats the full price as consideration, including any lien the buyer assumes.

  • A declaration of value, signed by at least one buyer or seller, goes to the county recorder with the deed.
  • Personal property is presumed part of the price unless its value is stated on the instrument.
  • Property tax on Iowa homes runs a year behind and is billed in September and March.
  • A seller closing from July 1 to December 31 owes the September installment, and one closing from January 1 to June 30 owes the March one.

An as-is cash sale does not change these rules. It changes who pays for repairs and how fast the deal closes.

faqs.q: Is there a capital gains tax in Iowa?
faqs.a: Iowa has no separate capital gains tax. Gains are part of Iowa taxable income, which is taxed at a flat 3.8 percent for tax year 2026.

faqs.q: Do I pay Iowa tax on the sale of my primary residence?
faqs.a: Only on gain above the exclusion. Iowa generally follows the federal rule that lets you exclude up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the ownership and use tests.

faqs.q: Can I deduct capital gains on a rental house sold in Iowa?
faqs.a: Not under the old non-farm real property deduction. The Department of Revenue says that deduction was repealed for tax years starting January 1, 2023, apart from installment sales begun before then.

faqs.q: Does Iowa tax gain when I inherit and sell a house?
faqs.a: Gain is measured from the stepped-up basis, usually the fair market value at the date of death. If you sell at about that value, little gain results.
